analysis.one_liner: Cuts sulfur dioxide emissions from coal-burning power plants across 31 eastern states by 10 million tons.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a hearing or a vote: introduced in May 1989 with zero cosponsors, it was referred to committee and two subcommittees and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to require a 10-million-ton reduction in sulfur dioxide emissions below 1980 levels in a 31-state region east of the Mississippi, done in two phases by 1997 and 2002. Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the main cause of acid rain, which damages lakes, forests, buildings, and health. States would write their own reduction plans, with a federal backstop forcing polluting power plants to cut emissions to 1.2 pounds of sulfur dioxide per million Btus if states failed to act. The bill also would have pressured Canada to make matching cuts and tied approval of electricity imports from Canada to Canadian progress.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants, especially in the Northeast and the Adirondacks of New York, would gain cleaner lakes, forests, and air. The bill named protecting employment as a goal and allowed flexible compliance methods — fuel switching, coal cleaning, energy conservation, and emissions trading — to soften costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the 31-state acid deposition impact region to cut annual sulfur dioxide emissions by 10 million tons below 1980 levels, with the first 5 million tons gone by January 1, 1997 and the rest by 2002.

Applies a federal emission standard of 1.2 pounds of sulfur dioxide per million Btus to major power plants in states that fail to adopt enforceable reduction measures, with penalties for sources that stay out of compliance.

Lets states and utilities use cost-effective compliance methods — emissions trading, early plant retirement, energy conservation investments, coal cleaning, and fuel switching — instead of mandating a single technology.

Directs the EPA, Energy, Commerce, and State Departments to pressure Canada into comparable sulfur dioxide cuts, and blocks approval of electricity imports from Canada until the EPA certifies Canadian progress.

Funds a research program, including long-term monitoring of acid damage to waters by a university or nonprofit facility with at least 30 years of data, to target the second phase at the most sensitive areas.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning electric utilities in the 31-state region would bear the cost of emission controls or fuel switching, and those costs could be passed to electricity ratepayers. High-sulfur coal producers would face weaker demand; the bill responded by allowing coal-cleaning compliance methods and stating a purpose of protecting current employment levels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-burning utilities and high-sulfur coal mines

drawbacks.text: The bill front-loads research and holds the second 5-million-ton reduction hostage to evaluations running through 1997, so full cuts would not be complete until January 1, 2002 — a decade and a half of continued acid deposition.
The 1980 baseline excludes emissions from sources built or converted after 1980 from state reduction requirements, so growth in electricity generation after 1980 would not add to the required cuts.

States and sources may substitute reductions in nitrogen oxides for required sulfur dioxide cuts at a rate of 2 units of NOx per unit of SO2, a flexibility that could shift rather than reduce total acid-forming pollution.

Control costs on utilities would ultimately be paid by ratepayers in the affected states, and the bill's own stated purpose of protecting current employment levels acknowledges the pressure on coal-dependent communities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A 10-million-ton sulfur dioxide cut would have delivered real, lasting relief from acid rain to lakes, forests, and communities downwind of coal plants, at a genuine but manageable cost to utilities and ratepayers — the bill tried to soften that cost with flexible compliance, emissions trading, and a research-informed second phase. Its weaknesses are the built-in delays (full cuts not until 2002), the 1980 baseline that ignores later emissions growth, and the NOx substitution option. On balance the design is protective, but slower and softer than a straight mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee never took the bill up; after referral to two subcommittees in June 1989, it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Solomon, a Republican from upstate New York — the Adirondack region hit hardest by acid rain — introduced the Acid Deposition Act on May 16, 1989.

The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and on June 26, 1989 was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment and the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No further action ever occurred: the bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or Senate consideration before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities and high-sulfur coal producers were spared the compliance costs this bill would have imposed. The public continued to absorb acid rain damage through this Congress; Congress did go on to enact acid rain controls in the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which became law after this bill had already died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal utilities and sulfur coal producers

for.name: Rep. Gerald B. H. Solomon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Acid Deposition Act on May 16, 1989 to require a 10-million-ton sulfur dioxide reduction in the 31-state eastern region.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its May 1989 referral, never scheduling a hearing or markup; it was passed to two subcommittees on June 26, 1989 and never advanced further.

against.name: Coal-burning utilities and high-sulfur coal interests
against.role: Regulated industries opposing acid rain control mandates in this era
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory sulfur dioxide reduction legislation generally during the 1989-90 debate over acid rain controls.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded supporter was a single Republican from acid-rain-affected upstate New York, and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would force utilities burning high-sulfur fuel in 31 eastern states to cut sulfur dioxide emissions to 1.2 pounds per million Btus or retire, clean fuel, or trade allowances. Their compliance costs would ultimately reach ratepayers, but the reductions are the point of the bill — cleaner air for everyone downwind.

Mandated sulfur cuts would reduce demand for high-sulfur coal. The bill partially cushions this by allowing precombustion coal cleaning and fuel substitution as compliance methods and listing employment protection as a purpose.

Fuel substitution is an approved compliance method, so utilities switching to lower-sulfur fuel would shift demand toward low-sulfur coal and cleaner fuels — a gain that runs directly alongside the public's interest in fewer emissions.

The bill authorizes emissions reduction banks and brokerage institutions to facilitate trading of reduction requirements, creating a new market whose growth depends on — and enforces — the emission cuts themselves.
